utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Our apologies for the delayed start. The Chamber was occupied by another matter, and we should now call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manning. Welcome back to the courtroom. Make yourself comfortable. Please be reminded that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir has more questions for you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May there be peace unto this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Greetings to Mr. Manning. May we resume where we stopped yesterday than was the issue of the transfer of authority from the OTP to the Bosnian -- or, rather, Federal Commission for Missing Persons. This is my question: Did you perhaps remember based on which document it was that you participated in the transfer of authority over exhumations to the Commission for Missing Persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tolimir. No, I did not remember anything more about that document, and I have not seep a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, if you will allow me to, I'll remind you of your statement in the Popovic case on this score. On page 18913 of the transcript, you said, and I'm quoting, explaining your role in the process of the transfer of authority to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, you said: "At the time, we created a small ICTY team to follow the exhumations conducted by the Bosnians. I was responsible for the team and was there to assist the team out in the field?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the document, 65 ter 0675. It should be displayed on the screen to enable the witness to see it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can document 65 ter 0675 be shown in e-court for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Mr. President, I -- if I may be of assistance, it's document P1818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18913.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the document should not be broadcast because it's confidential. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't think so. We should have the public redacted version of this transcript on the screen and not the -- that part under seal. That might be another number. I don't have the numbers yet, the P numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the public version of that document is P1819. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We need page 18913. There we have it on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, you've had an opportunity to read now what your testimony in the Popovic case was. This is my question: When you refer to the Bosnian commission in your testimony here, are you referring to the Federal Commission for Missing Persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know the body to be Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. From memory, it was a triumvirate, if you like, from the three parties involved, so it was a Bosnian Muslim, the Serbs, and the Croat entities which were looking at human remains all across Bosnia. But it was the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons that I dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, then, at the exhumations in Srebrenica in all the Srebrenica-related cases, did the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs participate in them, or was it only the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, prior to the hand-over in 2001, the exhumations were conducted by the ICTY, except for 2006, when it was the ICTY and PHR, Physicians for Human Rights. To the point of hand-over, no other entities from the former Yugoslavia were involved in that process. In fact, they were excluded from entry to the sites, and they were not involved in that process, whatsoever. Following the hand-over to the Bosnian government, they were responsible for the exhumations. Initially, we monitored in 2001 those exhumations, and thereafter it was ICMP who monitored the work of the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons in exhuming the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbs and Croats participate together with the Muslims in the exhumations of the victims related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there were any Serbs or Croats involved in the team. I think I recall a Croat archaeologist. But as far as I recall, it was a team predominantly controlled and made up of Bosnian Muslims from the Sarajevo and Tuzla area, and ICMP was an international body made up of many nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you don't know, but here we can read from your testimony, "I was responsible for the organisation of the team and to assist the team out in the field." We don't want it to appear here that the team was a multi-national one. Can you tell us the Bosnian commission, did it involve the participation of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my coordination was of the ICTY team who monitored the Bosnian commission team, so, effectively, they were ICTY employees. An archaeologist, crime scene officer and a photographer. They were the team that I was referring to. But as far as I know, the exhumations following 2001 were conducted by a Bosnian team, a Bosnian Muslim team. I don't recall there being a representative from one of the other entities. I believe it was just a Bosnian Muslim commission who were exhuming the Srebrenica bodies in the Srebrenica area. But that should be put to the Bosnian commission. And if I may, the team in 2001 that we monitored, was Mr. Murat Hurtic [realtime transcript read in error "Hutic"], and his team were effectively recovering the bodies. They were taking the bodies from the ground and taking them to Tuzla, to the mortuary, to be examined or -- or for a time to the ICTY mortuary to be examined. And from my recollection, they were all Bosnian Muslims employed by Mr. Hurtic and the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what Mr. Hurtic did during the war and whether he was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he probably was. I can't recall. He -- he was, I'm sure, a member of the military. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the witness state the name of the gentleman clearly? Can he spell it out perhaps because I as I heard it, it sounded different from what we have now in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the transcript we have, sir, "Murat Hutic".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, his first name was Murat M-U-R-A-T. His family name was H-U-R-T-I-C. Or ch, I apologise for my pronunciation. Murat Hurtic. Hurtic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In fact there was only the R missing in the family name. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, witness, and Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the commission led by Mr. Hurtic include also the president of the commission for missing persons, Mr. Amor Masic -- Masovic? Thank you. Let me shorten my question, was Amor Masovic a member of Mr. Hurtic's team? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think Mr. Masovic was, if you like, his supervisor, based in Sarajevo. I dealt with Mr. Masovic over a number of years. I believe he would have supervised Mr. Hurtic's work but during that period I dealt with Mr. Hurtic. Your Honours, I believe yesterday Mr. Tolimir asked me a question about allegations against Mr. Masovic and I did recall an allegation that I was aware of from conversations. Without casting any aspersions on Mr. Masovic, the allegations that I recall was that he had sold bodies during the war to the opposite side, but it struck me that I recalled that, and I should relay that to the Court. And I have no more information about that allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Tell us, why did the OTP and you personally entrust Mr. Hurtic with this work, as well as his supervisor, Amor Masovic, as they were a party to the conflict? Why were they entrusted with the entire effort of the exhumations and search for the victims of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately the responsibility for recovering the bodies was handed to the Bosnian government. They chose the mechanism to do that. Mr. Hurtic was involved in that process for many years. I have no doubt as to Mr. Hurtic's integrity and his honesty. I didn't choose to work with him, but I was pleased to do so. Mr. Masovic, I had less to do with. The decision as to who within the Bosnian government or what agency within the Bosnian government exhumed those bodies was, I assume, a decision by that government. We, as a Tribunal, handed over responsibility for the recovery of the bodies and we sought to monitor that process, and when we stopped monitoring that process, it was monitored by an international commission, the ICMP, who, to my knowledge, were present at all the exhumations and during the autopsy process and were in charge, effectively, of the DNA project.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, can you tell us when was it that you personally, as well as the ICTY, turned over the work to a mono-ethnic agency that was a party to the conflict whilst you distanced yourself from it all? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question involves some issues but when I handed over -- we handed over responsibility to the Bosnian commission, it was in 2001, I think early in the year. I would have to check the document. To characterise us handing it to mono-ethnic agencies, that's correct. It was monitored by an international agency. I don't know that the Bosnian commission was party to the conflict. I can't answer that part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell us when was it that you, as the ICTY, stopped following their work? And when did the representatives of the International Commission for Missing Persons take them over, as it were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from memory, we continued monitoring during 2001, and then we withdrew that team and it was monitored by ICMP. I believe that ICMP were involved with the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons well before that. I can't give you specifics, but they were involved with the Bosnian commission for some years prior to 2001. And following this -- the cessation of our monitoring, we still regularly visited the grave-sites, we still reviewed the material and the information that was coming from the Bosnian commission and ICMP for many years thereafter, and I would suggest we still do so, in seeking DNA data from ICMP and updates to reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Why did the ICTY withdraw from the monitoring process in 2001; and why did it hand over the work to an entity that wasn't a component part of the ICTY? Because the ICMP is just that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all the specific reasons, but effectively we had reached a point where we could no longer sustain that level of work. There were other trials and other investigations within the Tribunal. It was several million dollars each year. It was a massive project. I'm not saying that it simply came down to cost, but as the investigation matured, as the information that we had was collated, I believe that we reached a point where we couldn't sustain that level of work for the Tribunal. We also had several trials that were running, and eventually it reaches a point where you have to concentrate on other matters, and our work in the exhumations takes a very long time, and I think we would still be exhuming graves now if the ICTY continued with that work. To hand it over to the Bosnian commission meant that the bodies could be recovered, the work of identifications would continue at a much greater pace, and the families could have their loved ones' bodies returned to them. So it was a combination of all those aspects, but I can't remember a specific driver that -- that made us decide, or made the Tribunal decide that, as of now, we will cease doing exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether the International Commission for Missing Persons is a non-governmental organisation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the ICMP to be a non-governmental organisation. It's an international organisation which I think was sponsored or created by a former US politician. I understand that Queen Noor of Jordan was heavily involved in the funding and processing, and that it's an international organisation which is -- which -- whose mandate is to assist in identifying those killed in -- in wars and returning the remains to the family. Commission for Missing Persons is trying to establish what happened to the missing persons and assist the families. But it's best to ask that of ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you to explain who they were, just whether they were a non-governmental organisation. Please tell me, if you can, whether this non-governmental organisation and the State Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina have the responsibility to disclose to me, as an accused, both things that are damaging to me and things that are mitigating for me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last sentence of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters ask you to repeat the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do they have the responsibility towards this Court, as do representatives of the Tribunal? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is a consequence of what happened and the fact that you transferred authority to them the fact that people who died before 1995 are also on the list, as well as those who were killed after the events in Srebrenica in 1996 or 1998? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: ICMP's work extends right across the former Yugoslavia, as I understand it. It includes prior to Srebrenica and -- and events later than Srebrenica. So the list you refer to, if that's with ICMP, they have the responsibility for all the missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since they're responsible for all the missing people, is it also their responsibility to list everybody who went missing in the area of the former Yugoslavia on the list relating to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I -- if I completely understand. But if they listed the people missing from Srebrenica, they would not list the people who were missing prior to or after the fall of Srebrenica, because it would not be the Srebrenica list. When I reviewed their material, I sought the data from ICMP which related solely to Srebrenica. They hold data for other events at other times, but if you -- if you say, a Srebrenica list, then that should reflect the identifications related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Manning. We are here only because of Srebrenica and not the former Yugoslavia, so please tell me why these commissions, and you personally, didn't participate in the discovery of surface remains in Srebrenica in July of 1995 -- of the fighting that took place in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained before I wasn't involved in the recovery of surface remains, I believe the Bosnian commission were. I know the Bosnian commission were, and I know that ICMP were involved in the collection of surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this piece of information. Do you know whether anyone that they collected on the surface, that any body that was found was shown to have been killed during fighting and not during the executions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I wasn't involved in that process. I didn't see the bodies. I did read some autopsy reports related to surface remains, but I can't remember the details, as I was concentrating on the Srebrenica mass graves. But I wasn't involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at something that you recall and we talked about yesterday. On page 10181, Mr. McCloskey asked you: "Is there any evidence that victims of the fighting were left in surface areas and then put into any of the mass graves?" And on the same page, 10181, you said: "No. There was no talk of that," et cetera. And then Mr. McCloskey, on page 10182 asked you whether it was possible that the bodies found along the road were buried together with these. And then you replied, also on page 10182, that it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- that is not correct. But I think, if I can add, my question was, is it possible that bodies along the road were buried at Glogova. Then I think it's largely correct without having to go through all the transcript. But not these, meaning all the mass graves. It was Glogova that was left out of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, are you able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the question was, is that correct? Yes, again referring to Glogova and the possibility that bodies in that area may have been put into that grave. I believe I also said that I would have thought if that happened, that it would be very few bodies, and that we would see a difference. But, yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. You gave your reply. And now my question is this: Was anyone killed in fighting during the events in Srebrenica, and are they on the lists of those men who were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were killed in fighting during the Srebrenica incidents. You've no doubt heard evidence of the column, and I accept that men were killed in fighting following the fall of Srebrenica. The question about the list, I am afraid you're going to have to repeat. Which list are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The list of the OTP regarding the victims of Srebrenica. Are any people, any bodies that were found on the surface, on that list?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to my reports, as I said yesterday, in my count of the DNA evidence and information from ICMP, I counted -- I said 12. I believe it's 14 bodies from Kozluk mass grave area, which were surface remains, and I did not count any other surface remains. I was not part of the recovery of the surface remains, but I included the 14 individuals from the Kozluk area for a number of reasons, which I've given in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also replied to Judge Mindua yesterday, on page 10191 when he asked you: "Did you also find bodies that were on the surface?" And then on page 10191, you replied: "We did not, because the bodies were one metre deep inside the ground." Please don't give me the same reply you gave to Judge Mindua. Did the Prosecution team examine graves on the surface at all?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We examined the mass graves that I've described, and I indicated that at two locations there were surface remains, but those surface remains were part of the mass graves. The one at Orahovac, I indicated had been pushed by a machine from the grave to an area outside the grave. The body parts at Kozluk were part of the mass grave. You could see them on the surface. So you could describe them as surface remains in that they were partly visible on the surface, but they were part of the mass grave. We did not collect surface remains from areas. We did not travel through the woods collecting body parts. We exhumed large mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning, I understood your reply. And my next question is this: Since a moment ago, and yesterday during the cross-examination, you heard that there were thousands of bodies found in -- as surface remains and they were not inside the mass graves, can you tell me -- and yesterday we're listening to Ruez's report on Bare. Can you tell me why the OTP did not represent these 600 bodies in Bare as bodies of people killed in combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a translation issue, but "thousands," of course, is not correct. I think 600 is the correct figure that's been used before. So I don't know what the glitch is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the OTP examined the mass graves. We didn't collect the surface remains. We didn't conduct autopsies on them. We weren't part of that process. So for my reporting, and I assume for other reporting from the Tribunal, we reported on matters that we were aware of. Mr. -- sorry, the OTP have also produced additional reports based on ICMP data, which I understand includes surface remains. I wasn't part of that. But in answer to your question, I didn't include it because we weren't involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But since you were a representative of the OTP, by now has the OTP published any reports on the surface remains that were found, the 600 that were found in an ambush and the others that Ruez is talking about, as well as those that you talk about who were killed in Baljkovica, where are those, as Mr. McCloskey says, hundreds of victims? Are they in any reports of the Prosecution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the most recent reports. I haven't read Mr. Janc's report, I haven't read the recent reports. That's a question you will have to ask the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Can you tell us, and you mentioned Baljkovica a moment ago and the victims in that column. Can you tell us whether you collected information on how many people were killed in combat during the breakthrough of the column on both sides, in the Baljkovica region along the confrontation line? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team examined statements, interviewed witnesses, and interviewed suspects, partly about those numbers, about how the people were killed, how the attacks happened. Information and evidence was collected, but, again, I'm not -- I'm not in a position to advise whether that has been reported on since.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did the Prosecution ask the Muslim side, Did you have a single man who was killed during the breakthrough in Baljkovica? And did they ask the Serbian side, Did you have a single man killed when the Muslim convoy came, et cetera? Did you, as an investigator, know whether the OTP did any of this, whether they collected any such information?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took statements from witnesses, and when I interviewed suspects, part of that process was certainly to talk about the column, who was killed, how they were killed. That was part of the process, and that work was continued by the Tribunal and other investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Manning, let's now look at 1D1 -- 373 in e-court, please. 1D373. And while we're waiting for e-court, the OTP is familiar with this document. It's a document from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 16 July when the breakthrough happened at the confrontation line and it was signed by the commander of the Bosnian army, Rasim Delic. I would like you to look at the date, it's the 16th of July. And then I would like to have the last page so that can you see that he it was signed by the army commander, Rasim Delic. That's page 4, so could we --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Just for the record, this document has been admitted into evidence as D155, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at page 4 so that the witness could see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see that this was written by the commander, Rasim Delic, and that the accuracy of the information was certified. Could the witness please be shown page 3 of the document now. And the final item 3 on page 3, that's all we're interested in. There we go. You can see item 3. Please zoom in so the witness could read it. In English, it's page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to wait for the English translation. I think it's a very experienced witness, but I don't know if he has the skills to read the B/C/S text. I think we should zoom in on the top --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the top of the English page. There's the item number 3. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will read item 3 on this page, both in the English and the B/C/S. "Units of the 28th Division of the ground forces are pulling out of Srebrenica while still fighting. They have remained compact. In the temporarily occupied Territorial Defence, they have scored success after success. They have inflicted great losses on the aggressor. So far, they have eight Chetniks alive in captivity. Units of the 28th Division of the KoV have linked up with the infiltrated units of the 2nd Corps. Their joint forces have continued fighting in the temporarily occupied territory. It is expected that they will fully link up with these units. Activities are under way to exploit the success of units carrying out the breakthrough." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have seen army general, Rasim Delic, taking about this break through and he sent this report to Alija Izetbegovic. So he wrote this under full responsibility. Please tell us, whether the OTP knew at all that there was combat in the sector where the Tuzla Corps infiltrated the territory of the RS and the column that was trying to break through from Srebrenica to Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have already indicated that I accept that there was fighting. There's details that the column was armed at the front of the column, and I've certainly read and spoken to people who indicated there was combat. I accept that there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Were there any victims in this fighting on either side? And should they be recorded as victims related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough about how those people died, the ones that died in combat or the ones that were killed. I do know of accounts where men surrendered and were executed. I have seen that within the mass graves. Where -- where I could report on that, such as the contents of a mass grave where people have been bound and blindfolded and shot, I have reported on. I can't report on material that I didn't examine, and I didn't examine the battle-fields or the route of the column. Whether they're victims of Srebrenica, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Let us now look at -- I'm sorry. Page 931004/12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, before we leave this document on the screen, I would like to ask the Defence for an update about translations. I -- we noted that the Registry told us this document on the screen is D155, marked for identification, pending translation. To my surprise, there is a translation. We would appreciate if the Defence, like the Prosecution, would update us in a timely manner about uploading of translations. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the translation was updated into e-court very recently. Our practice is that we tender documents only after we've checked the translation. As for this document, the translation has been uploaded and we would like to tender it and have the marked for identification lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I'm not sure if you are correct. You tendered it. The Defence tendered it. It wouldn't have a D number. D155. It was marked for identification, pending translation, because the Defence tendered it. Now it will be D155, no longer pending translation. Mr. Tolimir, please continue. Mr. Gajic. I think you agree. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to apologise for not seeking to tender the document. Can we look at transcript page 93100, lines 4 to 12 of this trial, where a witness was talking about this conflict. That's the transcript of 2 February 2011. Thank you. We can't see it yet, so I don't want to ask my question until the transcript is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before this appears on the screen, tell us, did the OTP talk to the eye-witnesses of the conflict at the separation line, at the point when the 3rd Corps entered the territory of Republika Srpska to meet the column moving from Srebrenica toward Nezuk? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke to witnesses. I can't say if those witnesses were in that specific area. We sought statements from the women who were transported from Tuzla, the children, the men who survived, the men who trekked to Tuzla. We took statements from Serbian soldiers, Bosnian Serb soldiers, my apologies, and we interviewed suspects about those matters. Specifically in that area, I don't know. We spoke to witnesses and people and sought the story from when they went to Srebrenica to when they left, or when they dealt with the column or the survivors, or the executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now we have page 9300, lines 4 to 12, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we have the relevant portion on our screen, you can see that the witness says that the Army of Republika Srpska, that's to say, his brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we need is page 9310; our apologies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 4, the witness says that there were some 40 or 42 fatalities in answer to my question and these were victims on the side of the Republika Srpska army. My question is this: If an army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, it is always helpful to be very correct. This is line 8, not line 4. Line 4 is your question, and the answer is at line 8. At a later stage of the trial, the parties and the Chamber must find the relevant portions, and therefore I always have to correct that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I can see it also mentioned here in line 12 where it says that there were 40 or 42 dead on the side of the VRS and that's why I'm putting the question to the witness in this way to save time. If the Army of Republika Srpska, who was located in trenches and was covered in that way, had 40 to 42 dead, can it then be presumed that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina should have had at least three times the number of victims, since they were not in any sort of shelter. They were out in the open. Did you collect any sort of information and have any knowledge about the numbers of casualties they had? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the short answer is no, I did not. That would be something that could be dealt with perhaps by the military analysts. I didn't deal with that issue, and I can't comment on the relevant ratios.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at what military analysts had to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show up 1D00596. 1D00596. In other words, 1D596. This is the testimony by Richard Butler in the Popovic case. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In answer to the question whether you knew that there were witnesses saying that there were a thousand to 2.000 individuals killed from the column as a result of combat, were you aware of this? "A. In the period between 18 and 20 July. "Q. Correct. "A. I am not -- not aware of the specific number but that particular number of 1.000 to 2.000 sounds reasonable, given the context of the combat that I'm aware of. "Q. And you're saying that, including all of the combat engagements, correct, as opposed to one isolated combat engagement? Would that be fair if I can understand what you are saying? "A. Yes. I think the 1.000 to 2.000 number would be reasonable with respect to the combat casualties starting from 12 July through to, effectively, 18 July." You just mentioned military experts. Mr. Butler is one. So my question is this: Do you know if the OTP's list refers to individuals referred to by Mr. Butler, namely 2.000 individuals killed in combat? Were they included, as such, in the list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have already answered the question. In my list, in the list that I prepared, it related to the bodies recovered from the mass graves. It did not relate to surface remains or individuals involved in combat. And I'm not a military analyst and I'm not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a representative of the OTP at the time, the OTP being responsible for investigating into the cause of death of all the victims related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the OTP. I was involved in the investigation of the allegations arising from the fall of Srebrenica, and I examined specifically the details in relation to the exhumation of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber which representative of the OTP was charged with the victims referred to by the OTP expert witness, Mr. Butler? And I'm referring to the portion of the transcript we've just been looking at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't answer that question. I don't know whether you're referring to allegations of crimes committed at that time. We did examine the incidents, the whole picture of the Srebrenica -- the fall of Srebrenica, and part of that was an examination of the military aspects. I wasn't involved in that. I'm not a military expert. I examined and was part of the exhumation process, as well as taking statements and interviews from witnesses and suspects, which certainly touched on those elements, but I don't know who specifically investigated the numbers that Mr. Butler was talking about, and Mr. Butler was saying 1.000 to 2.000 as an estimate, I understand. I don't know if you're saying that there was a specific allegation about a thousand individuals. I can't help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours who the military expert was in the OTP team and can you tell us what your field of expertise was as a member of that team. What I mean is your professional background. Are you an anthropologist, a pathologist? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the military analyst team from the OTP, I think were all heavily involved in the investigation at some stage. Mr. Butler was certainly involved. Ms. Brettell was a significant part of that team. My expertise, as I've indicated to the Chamber and in my CV, I'm a police officer. I have been since 1983. I have been involved in police operations, investigations. Apart from two years of conducting senior management training, I have been an operational police officer in four, five countries, plus Australia, and I'm currently a representative of the Australia law enforcement agencies in the Middle East. I can provide further details, but I believe I have provided a curriculum vitae previously to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not interested in that, since it is not related to Srebrenica. This is what I'm interested in. What was the basis on which all the victims that were listed as victims of the mass graves were tied in with the events at Srebrenica and the related executions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mass graves that I've spoken about contain the remains of people, men and boys from Srebrenica, from the area of Srebrenica, who were killed, who -- who predominantly surrendered and were executed and placed there mass graves. The link to Srebrenica, I gave evidence previously. Those bodies and those individuals were linked to Srebrenica, and they have been identified since, particularly via DNA, as having been reported missing following the fall of Srebrenica. Also linked from survivor and witness accounts, the accounts of Mr. Erdemovic, and the analysis of all the forensics for the exhumation/autopsy process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Were bodies also buried in the mass graves which were surface remains collected from the locations where there was combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my understanding, the witness has answered this question already several times, yesterday and today. It's not helpful for anybody, especially not for the Defence case, just to repeat several times the same question. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What matters to me is that you, as the Trial Chamber, understand what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why do you frequently in your report refer to the "Srebrenica victim"? In selecting that term, do you mean it to refer only to those who were killed in Srebrenica in 1995, regardless of whether they were killed in combat or in any other way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my reports, I refer to the individuals located in the mass graves. I say a victim of the massacres following Srebrenica, the genocide from Srebrenica, the killings, the executions. I'm referring to individuals who were killed, who were murdered following the fall of Srebrenica, who were Muslims who were from Srebrenica and who were predominantly captured, or surrendered, by the VRS forces in the area and who were systematically killed. They were victims of what happened following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How many were there of such victims? And who was not deemed to belong to that category of victims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check my 2007 report, but since that time the DNA results have increased the number, I'm sure, significantly. But my reports provide a count of the number of victims found in the mass graves who were killed following the fall of Srebrenica, who were murdered. That number has -- as I say, has increased. I think -- if I could check my reports, but I think it more appropriate to have the most updated number which has been presented to the Chamber. But we -- my reports were dealing with 4.000 individuals, and they are the identified victims of Srebrenica located in the mass graves exhumed by the ICTY, and also, in some cases, by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The victims you're referring to, were traces found on them of artillery weapons or only gun-shot wounds? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without checking the reports, a significant number were assigned a cause of death from gun-shot injury, gun-shot wounds. There were blast injuries which would be consistent with either explosives, such as hand grenades, or RPGs. Some who simply were described as blunt force trauma, as in a crushing injury. And others who were assigned a cause of death of unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you place all of the victims that you exhumed from mass graves on the list of those killed, as you put it, in genocide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of people exhumed from the Srebrenica mass graves -- I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure if I understand the question. Again, the lists and the numbers that I reported on are individuals who have been removed from mass graves connected to the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in the mass graves, you found victims who died as a result of hand grenades and other assets, not just gun-shot wounds. Now, those victims which had gun-shot wounds on them, did you consider them to be the victims of executions and, as a consequence, were they put on a list of those killed in -- as part of a genocide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Where the pathologist or anthropologist could determine that the gun-shot injuries were consistent with, say, being shot in the back, or being shot through the blindfold, or being shot, in once instances, the feet, the knees, the hips, the elbows, the shoulder and the head, or the individuals who were shot at Glogova, those instances where they could definitively say that those individuals were shot in that manner, they included that in the autopsy reports. In relation to the blast injuries, I recall that many of those were associated with the Kravica warehouse, where the survivors indicated grenades were thrown into the warehouse and also a rocket-propelled grenade was fired through the warehouse. We, in fact, found parts of that rocket-propelled grenade in the grave at Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard from pathologists in this case that shrapnel from artillery weapons was found as well. Did you list victims that had shrapnel in them among the victims of genocide? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure that I can comment on the evidence of the pathologists about shrapnel from artillery weapons. I recall shrapnel injuries associated with hand grenades because we found parts of hand grenades, of a rocket-propelled grenade. I can't recall finding a piece of an artillery shell or establishing that that -- that shrapnel was from an artillery shell, but I would have to check through the pathology reports and the expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court is aware of that. Did you list all the victims related to Srebrenica as victims of genocide? No, no, as -- by the same token were all those victims wearing civilian clothes listed as civilians?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we didn't list the victims as civilians or make a particular definition. Some of the victims had military clothing or pieces of military clothing. I don't recall ever seeing a victim in a complete uniform. The majority of the victims wore normal clothing, but I certainly accept some of those individuals had some items of military clothing. And statements from the survivors and the column members indicate that some of the members of the column who surrendered were members of the Bosnian Muslim army. I accept that a significant number, perhaps, of the people in the graves were members of the Bosnian military who surrendered and were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that members of the BH Army who were present in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica wore civilian clothes, in order to pass unnoticed or pass off as civilians, in the presence of UNPROFOR forces patrolling the area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there were witnesses interviewed by OTP investigators who said that they had worn civilian clothes in order that our activities may not be observed by UNPROFOR? Were you aware of these witness statements? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your reports, did you state that you did not find any indications that would point to the presence of military personnel among the victims in mass graves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the contrary. Where we found something that indicated a military personnel, we would report it. It would be in the autopsy report. I think I have mentioned in evidence that one individual had a pistol in his belt. I recounted a story, which I wasn't part of, where a grenades was found within a uniform shirt at the mortuary. I saw, as I said before, some items of a military uniform on some of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find in the graves military documents indicating that at the time of the individual's death, they were members of the BH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check, but perhaps within the identifications you would have found a military identification. But witness accounts and survivor accounts indicated that -- that the -- that victims were members of the BiH military, some of them. I can't recall specific military documents. Certainly there weren't orders or any detailed military documents that we found, but we may have found military IDs. I would have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's now the time for the first break. It's 10.30. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I ask you, if you are tendering the documents you used. I'm referring to 1D596. This is part of the transcript, I hope only a part of the transcript with the testimony of Mr. Butler. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, we would like to tender that document. It is only one page from the testimony of Mr. Butler in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned exhibit number D168. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We talked about, before the break, and my question would relate to that, during the exhumations that the teams were doing at the locations that you listed, did you come across any military documents, such as, for example, military orders and others, which would show from where they originated?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not, to my memory. As I said before, we may have found military identification documents. I don't recall specifically, but no orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we show the witness Exhibit P1071, 1071. It is a report by Dr. Haglund on the exhumations that was carried out at Cerska. It's page 65 in the English, and page 70 in the B/C/S. We will see a table, which lists the artefacts that were used and that were buried in this mass grave under CSK-42. Once we zoom in, we will see Mujo Omanovic under this number. And military orders were found on him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These tables are so small -- Mr. Tolimir, these tables are so small. Perhaps it's for the benefit of the witness only necessary to have it in English on the screen. Would that be sufficient for your purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can show it for the witness. It's important for the witness to see it. Thank you. Thank you. I apologise, if we look from underneath you will see a name, Osmo Muminovic. Military orders were found on Osmo Muminovic and we can also see in this table that a military identification card was found on Ajisa Memisevic. He is number 6 on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what I just read from this report by Mr. Haglund, can you tell us, whether you, as an investigator, were familiar with these military documents and that some of the bodies found in the mass graves had military identity card and other documents that would show their affiliations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said, I would have to check the reports. If you look at my report from 2000, I would have listed the artefacts recovered from Cerska 142, which is Mr. Muminovic. I can't recall now the condition of the document. It may be that it was unreadable, but we could certainly find a photograph of that item. And, as I say, I examined those artefacts which were located in the -- the graves, and I believe I would have recorded details of those documents in my 2000/2001 report. And as I said before, I did recall military identification cards. I don't recall that particular military order, in which -- if it was readable, would have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we'll show you your report from 2000, which is P1825. That's your report from 2000. But before that, let me ask you one question. Since this is Cerska, and since there was combat in Cerska before, is it possible that these documents indicate that these victims died in an earlier period or in the period when Srebrenica fell in July of 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I think 150 individuals in the Cerska grave were -- the majority of them were bound, and they were shot at Cerska and buried on the side of the road at Cerska. So the individuals at Cerska, undisturbed primary mass grave, were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have your report. It's P1825. Could we have page 35 in B/C/S and page 38 in English. It is a summary that relates to Cerska, and the title is: Identifications. First of all, tell us, why did you compile this report? Before we look at its contents.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to prepare this report by Senior Trial Attorney Mark Harmon. It was a report as a summary of the forensic evidence to be presented, then, in the Krstic case, and thereafter, in other cases. And I produced it as a summary, as a link, as an encompassing document, in relation to the exhumations and autopsy reports -- autopsy examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it have been better for the Court if you -- if this report had been compiled by expert pathologists or anthropologists instead of policemen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. The pathologist, anthropologists, archeologists, other forensic experts prepared detailed reports, as experts. That group of reports was at least 50 reports, multi-volume reports. I was asked to review all that documentation, all those reports, all the photographs, more than 60.000 colour photographs, more than 10.000 physical artefacts, all the written documentation spanning the entire project and link those reports and the artefacts, photographs, items, and documentation in a summary. It is that, a summary, and the underlying reports, the pathology report, the archaeological reports, the forensic reports can all be examined. I took the information from those reports, or I physically examined the material in the report, the documentation, the bodies, the photographs and produced this report and other similar reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us during the trial of Mr. Krstic was your report used or were reports written by pathologists and anthropologists as well that you talked about, based on which then the summary was compiled?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both were used. The experts were called to give evidence in person. Their reports were tendered, and I presented my report and tendered into evidence, from memory, about 40 Lever arch files of supporting material, including the reports of the experts, photographs, documentation, pathology, anthropology reports, and individual autopsy reports. So both the experts gave their evidence and I gave evidence based on that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could we look at a part of this report that relates to identification. We should look at the second paragraph from the bottom under the heading: Identification. Both in the Serbian and in the English. I will read the paragraph because I consider it to be relevant and I quote: "During the exhumation and autopsy process, 22 useable identification documents, items were located. This included identity documents, official court documents, personal papers and a cigarette tin ... these items are further detailed in Annex C," which is on page 98 in e-court, both in the Serbian and the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to page 98. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksander. I'd like to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see it, and as for Osmo Muminovic. You are only listing a driver's licence. Do you not mention the military orders and you're not mentioning his identity card. And the identity card is a basic identification document. So my question is: How do you explain this discrepancy between what is in your report and what's in Dr. Haglund's report that we quoted a moment ago? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, without physically going and checking the items, the photographs of the items, I indicate in the report, useable identification documents. It was the case in almost every grave that documents were found on the -- on the bodies. Photographs, driver's licence. As part of the removal process, we tried to protect those documents. I saw photographs come out of the grave where you could see the face of an individual and as it was exposed to air that image disappeared, you had a blank photograph. When you opened a piece of paper that had been in a -- in the ground for several years amongst rotting corpses, amongst body fluids, amongst ground water, the documents were very often destroyed and even when opening the documents you would lose the image, the writing immediately. And if they were stored for a lengthy period they would deteriorate. Now, in my report, I said useable identification documents. It may be that that particular document, by the time I examined it, and, remember, this is 1998, 2000, and this grave was exhumed in 1996, the document had deteriorated to a point where it could not be used. It could be, and I would need to check, that the reference from Dr. Haglund's report, his notes, were taken from a body which was removed from the ground in the field and was covered in mud and dirt and they opened the document and they said it was a driver's licence and a military order. It was then examined at the mortuary in better conditions. They might have then discovered that, in fact, it was a military driver's licence, or it was a driver's licence that indicated his occupation was a military officer. Without checking, I can't tell you what that particular document was. But there's a photograph of that document, there's a photograph of the -- of the remains identified as Cerska 142, and can you see what was recovered from the body. And in this instance, I've referred to a useable identification document, something capable of assisting in identifying that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at Table 1, the -- on the right-hand side of the screen, the second name from the top where it says CSK-142, Osmo Muminovic. I said that Dr. Haglund said CSK-142, military orders were found on Osmo Muminovic and we can also see in this table that a military identity card was found on Ajisa Memisevic, and instead of military, you say identification card. Did these mistakes happen by accident in your report and the entries by the anthropologist, and are you allowed to change the name -- names of the artefacts found?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't changed the artefacts found. I have listed the useable identification documents. And I said that in my report, which was these documents may assist in identifying these victims. And that material would have been used by PHR, at that time, to identify the victims. I've indicated in here that the driver's licence on CSK-142, Mr. Muminovic would be capable of assisting in identifying him. The military identification document may have been in such poor condition that you could not read it. It would therefore not assist in identifying that individual. I've listed here the item that I thought would assist in identifying him. If you look at the autopsy report for body 142, will you see listed the items that were located on that body. You will see photographs of those items. We could examine those items and see whether you can read them. In my recollection, is that we couldn't read those documents; otherwise, I would have listed them here. And if you remember, very much a part of our work was to try and identify these people, so it was very important for me to find material who that identify these people. That, A, would show who they were, that they were from Srebrenica; B, that we could seek to interview people who knew them and could explain to us why they were found in a mass grave in the area of Srebrenica; and also return those human remains to the families. So if I could find an identification document that would assist in identifying that person, I would list it here. If it wasn't of use, I didn't list it. But it is recorded in the Tribunal documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add a question to that. In fact, what was the purpose to create this list and Annex C, especially with the headline: Identification items. What was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my summary, I sought to give an overview of the graves and the execution points, so I, along with Mr. Harmon, said what would be important, details of when the grave was exhumed; who exhumed it; how many bodies; the sex; the age determination; the cause of death; religious affinity, were they Muslims, were they another religious group, another ethnic group and, of course, identifications. So if you see at the bottom of that table is religious items. Again, I was summarizing what was located which could support or refute that these were Muslims. So I have listed there items of a religious nature. In other parts of the report, I've listed the cause of death or the age determination or the sex determination. So it was to assist, hopefully, the Court in seeing the information in those aspects that we found amongst the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, that in these lists you didn't include all items found with a specific body but only those who have -- yeah. A purpose for identification or for determining the religious situation of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much, Your Honour. In relation to, say, Cerska 128, there may have been a comb, a flint, a house key, a cigarette lighter, photographs that had faded. Now I didn't list all those items because the list would have been tremendously long and it was already listed in the autopsy report and in the photographic logs and in other reports. So what I did was say, it's very important that we identify these people. Here is a list of things located within those bodies, or with those bodies which might assist in that. So I didn't -- I didn't list in this report all the other items. And if there was a document that was in such poor condition that you couldn't read it, then I wouldn't highlight it here, because it wouldn't be of use in identifying the person, or in the next section showing what religious affinity they may have. So this is a summary of what was available. But those are the reports, those are the details I presented into evidence in -- in those 40-odd folders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since this is very important to the Court, because in 1993 some people were killed in Cerska who might have been killed by other perpetrators and the military documents would show this. So it's not by accident that the identity card on person CSK-144 and on the person above him, CSK-142, the driver's licence and the ID card are listed as identification documents, there must a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So I would like to ask the witness to look at P10781 in English, page 65. I would like him to look at only the title so we wouldn't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we look at P10171, page 65 in the English -- in the English language. Could the witness please look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that can't be the right number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My legal advisor warned me. It's P1071. Could we please zoom in on the title and then read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Actually, I would like to ask the witness to read the title since he speaks English. Could he read it out loud for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the top much the document says: "Table 6, documents providing leads to tentative identification and results of DNA analysis for Cerska grave-sites, footnote 4."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think -- perhaps, you misspoke. There's a problem. The last word is "site" and not "sites," in plural.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, "site."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "Site." Thank you. I see there is -- I read Table 8. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I -- I can't -- perhaps it is Table 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in on the headline.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Table 8. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As we saw, Mr. Haglund, and if you look at number -- name number 4 from below, he lists the documents that are used for identification. Military documents and a military card. And this is not mentioned by the investigator, so that's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it because these came from 1993 or from 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was -- these documents aren't from 1993. The reason I didn't include those documents is because, as I said, they were not useable. They were available. They were presented into evidence. They were part of the supporting material for my report. If there was a document that indicated that individual was from 1993, I would have made a note of that. It would have been important. The individuals in Cerska were executed in July of 1995. If we had found a document on a body from that grave which said 1993, that would simply have indicated that he had a document from 1993 in his pocket. He was killed in 1995 and -- and covered with soil in the Cerska valley. Those individuals, the majority of whom were tied up, who were bound, were killed then and not in -- in previous battles, and not in another area and conveyed to that grave-site. And the suggestion that I would change the evidence and hide the evidence is completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not trying to impute anything to you here. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what was the procedure for filing the objects found in the graves and how can we find the military orders found during the exhumation of the Cerska grave-site so that the Trial Chamber itself can see whether these military orders were damaged or whether they were used in any way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process changed from 1996 to 2001, that effectively a record was made at the grave-site of the body and of the identification if it was found then. A record was made at the mortuary, I think in Kladanj at that time. There was a -- and I believe there would be more than one photograph of that item, and that photograph would be linked to Cerska 142. So within the records of the exhumation of that grave would be an autopsy report be detailing body 142, what was found on body 142, that would have been signed by the pathologist, anthropologist. It would have included links to the photograph of those items. There would be a photographic log which said, On such and such a date, a photo was taken of the items recovered from Cerska 142. And there would also be a brief description of that item, which may say, "identity card" or it may say, "military identity card". But those records are available, and, indeed, as I said, the autopsy reports from body 142 from Cerska was presented into evidence in Krstic trial, and I believe, in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. If a military ID card was found on the person which is listed here as third in this table and it was found on the person under number 142, can you tell us then whether this person was searched before the killing, if these documents, the military orders, had not been taken away from him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to indicate, on the document that I'm looking at Cerska 142 is not number three. But I can't say that they were searched and that document was missed. In my experience of seeing several thousand bodies, the majority had something in their pockets. The majority -- the vast majority did not have bags or suitcases or back-packs, but almost all of them had some items in their pockets, cigarette lighters, fire-starters, keys, photographs, and often more than one wallet in their pocket. I believe that they would collect the identifications from deceased persons and carry them. But I can't say whether they were searched. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. We don't have much time, so can we have in e-court P1776, page 97 in English, and 104 in Serbian. That's Mr. Brunborg's report dated 2009? I want to take a look at only one table, a table showing the discrepancy between the date of death or missing, between the lists of the Prosecution and the BiH Army. The table also contains information on the mass grave where the remains were found. So this is the table that we are interested in. Now can you take a look at the first three columns. That's the name, and then we have date of birth, date of death, and then date of death corrected, which means that somebody must have corrected it. And also you can see the place of death, corrected as well. Now when you have considered this table, you will see that some dates denote 1992. The last numbers will you see 92, 92 and but then there is 94, 94, 93, and so on and so forth. There are many, many numbers 92, 93, 93, 94, 95, 95, 94, 94, 92, 94, 94, 94, 95. So there are many victims here who were killed before the events in Srebrenica and as you can see some of those dates were corrected later on. So my question is: Can you please analyse this table a little bit further, if this is necessary and then tell me is it true that the data here show that some of the cases that the OTP is trying to link only with Srebrenica are also the cases which were actually killed before 1995, because they were buried before 1995. Could we maybe zoom in on the English table for the witness so that the witness could have a good insight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I wonder if this is the witness that should be testifying about this without further foundation that he knows what these documents are or anything about it. I know we have heard lots of evidence on this. But without a foundation -- further foundation what is the purpose of this witness's analysing documents in this manner, I don't see how it ties in to any of the topics that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we have heard Dr. Brunborg explaining this table. But perhaps the witness knows something about it. Please try to answer the question, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can say, I don't believe there's any instances where the bodies in the mass graves that I've spoken about pre- date July of 1995. There is no evidence whatsoever that any of those bodies that I've seen, pre-date 1995. As to this table, I've seen Mr. Brunborg's work. It is extraordinarily detailed. I cannot really comment on why that figure, those dates are there, or who supplied those dates. This work was done by Mr. Brunborg. I do note that it says this is a table of inconsistent results and identified the fact that those details must be wrong in some respect. And, indeed, some of them have been corrected to July of 1995. So I can't really assist in this particular table and the underlying data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. I didn't want you to comment on this. I merely asked you if you connect all those victims to the events in Srebrenica, wouldn't you agree that this data here shows that some victims perished in events which are unrelated to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness provided you with his knowledge about this table. He just gave the answer. There's no need for repeating the question. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you, Your Honour. We are going to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, certain reports have been tendered into evidence through you. Can we have 65 ter 533. This is a document titled: Witness statement, Antonio Brown investigator. Could you please tell us whether this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I interrupt you. We would like to have the clear -- a clear record, the Registrar please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 00533 is an exhibit, P1821. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That helps. Now your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Registrar. So can we have this on the screen. Okay. Now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is statement of witness. Since it says here: Statement of witness, is it a witness statement or is it an expert report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's both. Mr. Brown completed a report in a manner that was appropriate to his legal system. Professor Wright produced a completely different report. Mr. Baraybar, again, different, which, if I can comment, is one reason why I summarized the reports, because they were all in different formats, but without looking at the rest of the document this is a -- is a statement by an expert witness, Mr. -- sorry, Professor Anthony Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us any expert information on the methods used by palynologist during compiling of his report?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can as a layman. I assisted Mr. Brown. I collected samples with him. I went through his reports and his statements. Extraordinary interesting process. But I'm a layman. He explained the process to me, soil in a certain area is a product of the geography of that area. If it's in a river-bed, clearly, it will have large boulders and sand, et cetera. If it is at the top of a mountain, it will have a different geography and a different soil. Mr. Brown also relied on pollen. If an area has a number of willow trees, then willow pollen would be in the soil. If there's a horn beam, that would be in the soil. He also relied on micro-fossils within the soil, which, in total, indicated to him that the soil in that particular area was a product of the immediate geography. So he could say that the soil from Glogova had a certain characteristic. If you travelled 30 kilometres away the characteristics were different. He as an expert compared those differences and he would say that the soil in the secondary grave was the same indistinguishable from the soil in the primary grave, and that that soil did not belong in the area of the secondary grave. But, again, that's a layman's summary of Mr. Brown's expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this, for this layman's explanation of Mr. Brown's report. And now we can go to another topic that relates to the method of interviewing witnesses, more specifically, those interviews in which you took part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
