utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P147. This is the interview performed by Mr. Manning. The witness was Mr. Milorad Bircakovic. So can we have 1D147, page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just for the record, this is not in your list of documents to be used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Does that mean that we may or may not use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may use it. I just want to establish good working conditions for both parties. You may use it. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the record, this is exhibit D147. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we only take a look at the table because it contains both Serbian and English. My legal assistant just told me that we can use this copy because it contains both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm interested in the seventh row from the top. Can you take a look at the seventh row. It's page 19. Page 19, seventh row, please. Thank you. I'm going to read now from what I see in front of myself. You say: "We have aerial images of the executions taking [realtime transcript read in error "takes"] place." And then you say: "We have seized records from the Zvornik and the Bratunac Brigade." And then you say: "And we have many people from those brigades in the Drina Corps interviewed." And then you say: "We also have your documents, your documents from the military police, and your daily schedule." And then say: "What I want you to understand is that it's very important for you to tell the truth." And then you say: "If you try to hide what happened, or hide your part in what happened, your knowledge of what happened, I can prove that you lie, and I want you to understand that this is your chance to tell the truth, here and now," et cetera. Now, bearing in mind what you told the witness before you interviewed him, and later on you questioned him about other subjects - we can read about it later on in the text - and you told the witness that you exhumed bodies of thousands of men and boys before this interview with the witness. My question is as follows: Who was the team leader during the exhumation of mass graves of Branjevo and Orahovac, was it you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Branjevo Military Farm, it wasn't me; I wasn't at the Tribunal. In Orahovac, there was an exhumation that was conducted before I was there and I was present for the exhumation of Orahovac 2, an area that had been unexhumed. And I was present at not only the -- the location and the opening of Orahovac 1, but for most of the exhumation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you take a look at the 12th row from the top in this table. This is where you say: "I have personally exhumed bodies of thousands of men and boys." Does that pertain to the mass graves about which you questioned Witness Bircakovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I had been involved at that stage in the exhumation of a number of mass graves which contained thousands of bodies. And not only that, I dealt with the artefacts and the bodies from the previous exhumations for when I wasn't present. I'd returned hundreds of bodies to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, and I believe that I have the right to say that I was personally involved in the exhumation of thousands of men and boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You may have right to say anything, but would you please answer this question: This way of questioning a witness that we can see here, is it actually an extortion of statement, the statement in line with what you know to be true, or were you exactly supposed to ask him about his own knowledge and to obtain and -- those answers from him that he wanted to give you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from memory, the suspect was a relatively junior member of the corps. I recall that I cautioned him, that I gave him his rights, that I offered him a lawyer, that I offered him the opportunity to seek legal advice, and part of my duties as interviewing a suspect is to clearly tell them what I intend to question them about. I intend to question you about the Srebrenica executions; I intend to question you about your role in those executions. If I can then let that witness know, a relatively junior member of the corps, that we have a great deal of information, a great deal of evidence that showed what happened, I would hope that he would see that and understand that it would be in his interests to tell the truth, but, also, that I was seeking the truth. I did tell him that we had that information. I did tell him that we would be able to tell if he was lying, as many of the other suspects had done, and I wanted to make it very clear to him, in fairness to him, that we knew many of the circumstances of the offence, and if he lied to us, then it would not be providing the truth and it would not assist him, but I gave him his rights as a respect. I didn't, in any way, brow-beat him. If you listen to the tape on no occasion did I raise my voice. I simply stated factually what we knew, and that we had a significant amount of information and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you gave some facts to him and then later on questioned him on those very same facts, isn't there a danger that he could be led astray by those facts, instead of telling you his own answers? And now he is telling you something about the things that you actually found out through other people and other methods. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is something you would have to ask the witness. But if you look at this interview, I am assuming that it went on for several hours, and when I finished talking to the witness, to the suspect, I asked him if he could tell me his story, his version of the events. And he told me his version of the events, and I questioned him on every aspect of that version of the events. And I believe, without checking, that I showed him maps or documents or photographs to assist in that process. But I gave him the opportunity to answer my questions the way he wished to do. And if there was any discrepancy that I could see, I would ask him questions, Can you please explain to me your answer? Et cetera. I gave him the opportunity to tell me his story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. In line -- on page 48, line 7, General Tolimir, quoting from the document on the screen, has you as saying: "We have aerial images of the executions takes place," meaning, I suppose, "taking place." Do you have actually have images of executions taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one thing I would like to do is check the tape to see exactly what I said, but I do accept that I said, We have a aerial image or images of the execution taking place. I believe, without reading the entire document, I'm referring to the Branjevo Military Farm photographs, in which Mr. Erdemovic had described the bodies lying on the grounds and you see, in those images, bodies lying on the ground. I also believe I'm able to say that in we have photographs of mass graves being created at the time that people are killed, that people are executed. Now, I don't say that we have a photograph of a man standing with a gun and shooting someone, but we have photographs showing the execution of men and boys next to mass graves. We have mass graves created where we know people were executed. But in specific answer to your question, I believe I was referring to that image from Branjevo Military Farm. I would -- I would have to check when we received the video of the Kravica warehouse which shows bodies outside the warehouse and sound of gun-fire. I would have to check when we received that, because I might also have been referring to that, although it's not an aerial image. There is an aerial image of that bus that's photographed in that image. But, specifically, I believe I was referring to the Branjevo Military Farm image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. The Trial Chamber, in these proceedings, had the chance to see the statements of many Prosecution witnesses, and they could see that before giving the statement, the representatives of the OTP would give them the status of a suspect, both before the interviews and before their testimonies here in the courtroom. My question is: What are the specific conditions for somebody to be considered a suspect and then accorded the rights of the suspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm sure what General Tolimir is referring to is the caution that we normally give. But I don't think the term, as you remember, is suspect in that. So I just -- so the witness is clear, I'm not sure you've ever referred to anyone as suspect. But I think what the General is saying just the caution, just so that is clear, so the question is clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, gives this remark of Mr. McCloskey reason for rephrasing your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the course of my examination of Prosecution witnesses in this case, I would oftentimes ask them if they knew what was the basis for their suspect status. Even this witness was cautioned that he may be considered a suspect, which will depend on the answer he gives, and this also has to do with Witness Bircakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so my question for Mr. Manning was:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What were the conditions that needed to be in place in order for an individual to be considered a suspect, and in order for him to be cautioned accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's just a slight misunderstanding. I have no problem with the General's questions about suspects prior to interviews; that's absolutely correct. What he -- he suggested that the Court has referred to people as suspects, and that's just not correct. But there's something -- there's the caution that we know about which sounds much like that and I think that's what he is referring to. I just wanted to clarify that. Because it would not be correct to say that the Court has referred to people as suspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I didn't understand Mr. Tolimir in that way, that he was -- I think it was clear from the record and from this document that he was referring to such an interview of a witness by Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That -- I absolutely agree. But then he went on and said in Court they do the same, they do the same thing and that is what I understood him to say. And I think he meant the caution but, you know, I could be wrong. We can go back. He said it happens in the investigation and it happened in court. And that -- that's my only clarification. What happens in court is a caution, not a suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we can resolve the problem by asking the witness, what were the conditions that needed to be in place in order for a person to be considered a suspect or in order for him to be cautioned accordingly? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in each case, it would be different. Without reading the interview and my recollection of the circumstances, the suspect would have been identified as a suspect because of a suspicion that he was involved in the offence. Perhaps when the individuals were in the Zvornik Brigade engineering logs. Perhaps he -- we could identify that he was in a particular area. I can't tell you the specifics, but a suspect is someone who, for some reason, we suspect of having involvement in the offence. Major Jokic, for instance, who was tried previously, was identified from a duty log as being present in a certain place at a certain time, which would have led me to believe he was a suspect. In this case, something led us to believe he was a suspect, his involvement. I, therefore, cautioned him and gave him certain rights. If he was a member of the Serbia -- the Bosnian Serb Army, and I had no suspicion that he was a suspect, I would have interviewed him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just so you're absolutely clear, page 52, line 23, the question is about suspects and then he goes and says: "Both before the interview and before their testimonies here in the courtroom ..." And it was the "before their testimonies here in the courtroom", that -- I think he is just referring to the caution, which is very similar to the suspect interview, and that was my point. For the investigator, there is quite a big difference is why I wanted to get that straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I think we have overcome this problem. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The caution normally given in the courtroom is understood to be the same given by the Prosecution normally during interviews. At least that's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was the member on your team who decided if a person was to be accorded the status of a suspect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, we needed to summons these individuals. We would send an official summons to the Republika Srpska to request these suspects attend. So, we, as a team, would have made the decision that they were a suspect. Perhaps, I said this man was present on this day; therefore, he is a suspect. Do you agree? Yes. Let's summons him as a suspect. Someone else may have said, Here is a document that shows that this man was there; therefore, he is a suspect. But the request to have that person attend for interview was a formal request made by the Tribunal to the Republika Srpska. So it would vary as to who would indicate that the person was a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who was from among the team of investigators, the one authorised to make such an assessment and give the caution? Thank you. Or better said, who was it within the team who had the right to give the status of suspect to an individual.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, effectively, if it was a planned mission in advance, we would submit the documentation and ask for those individuals to attend. But if I spoke to a witness, perhaps I spoke to a witness in Tuzla, and that witness said to me, I killed someone, I would make the decision, based on what they said, that they are a suspect, stop the witness interview and start a suspect interview. I could make that decision as a police officer, as an investigator. But in the more structured process, we would discuss which individuals should be interviewed. We would discuss their status. We would have them come as a witness. You are a witness, sir, we would like to ask you questions, and take a witness statement. Or we would establish that for some reason they're a suspect, and we would conduct a suspect interview. And it could be, in that process that, at the end of it, I could say, well, that person is no longer a suspect or is less of a suspect or prove to me that they were not there. But I could make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted to hear, whether it was you, members of the team, who made that decision, or whether it was up to the OTP, as such, to grant a status of the sort before an interview -- an interview is conducted.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was both, Your Honours, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When an interview is summons and you -- when an individual is summonsed and the summons indicates that the individual is a suspect, do you have the obligation to tell the individual, before you commence questioning him, what the basis for the suspicion against him is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the wording of the summons. It may have indicated that. It may have indicated generally, that, as a member of a certain corps, they were considered a suspect. I don't recall. But as soon as I commenced the interview, I would tell them why they were a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, we saw Witness Bircakovic's statement. Did you caution him about the fact that he was considered a suspect, and did you tell him why this was so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I'd have to check. But if he was a suspect, I would have cautioned him, given him his rights and then said, I wish to speak to you in relation to your involvement in the Srebrenica massacre, or in your involvement in relation to Branjevo Military Farm, or whatever specific topic I was going to discuss with him. But I would caution him and then I would tell him, generally, the allegation against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this mean that the OTP would previously have specific information as to why a certain individual is considered a suspect? And was it then necessary for the individual to be given that specific information underlying suspicion, together with the rights that were read to the person?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I don't recall what the summons said, but when the person is interviewed, I would tell them, as is fair, what they were suspected of. That might be in general terms. For instance, I interviewed the commander of the artillery unit which shelled the town of Srebrenica. I had records which showed that he had shelled a significant -- fired a significant number of shells into Srebrenica. He was, therefore, a suspect, and I said to him, words to the effect of, I want to talk to you about the shelling of Srebrenica, your role in that. And, as it progressed, I would produce to him documents, showing how many shells were fired into Srebrenica, how many shells he had fired the previous day, asking him why he did that, what was the purpose of that. So as the interview progressed, you would become more and more specific and would you show the suspect what documents or photographs or witness accounts you had which indicated why they were suspects. It was a lengthy interview process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. Tell us, was it your practice to allow any of these individuals to retain a legal representative or a lawyer and would they have one present while you were interviewing them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were a suspect, they would be offered the opportunity of seeking legal advice, of getting a lawyer. And in many instances, a lawyer was present. If they initially refused and said, I don't need a lawyer, at any stage during the interview if they said, I think I need a lawyer, I would have stopped the interview and allowed them to get a lawyer. Some had sought previous legal advice; some had lawyers present; and I believe this individual, from memory, did not have a lawyer present. But he was given that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a single case where an individual who was told that he was a suspect ultimately became a suspect, or, alternatively, was charged with certain allegations but were then -- but then these charges were subsequently dropped in exchange for a statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. The charges wouldn't necessarily have been dropped if -- perhaps Mr. Erdemovic is a good example. He gave evidence after he was charged. I'm not quite sure if I have your question correct. But there were instances where people were interviewed as suspects, and then, later on, we believed they were not suspects. There were cases where people were interviewed as suspects and were later charged before this Tribunal or by the Bosnian Court. And there is a process where an individual can provide evidence to the Court after they've been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Erdemovic. After -- was he interviewed after the indictment was issued or did he ask for such a status after the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Was he interviewed before the indictment was issued or was such a status accorded after the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have met Mr. Erdemovic once. I wasn't involved in that process. I understood that he was brought to the Tribunal, was interviewed and was charged. I don't know that process, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I was about to ask you in those instances where you were present and where a suspect would ultimately become an indictee, if you have any such experience in the cases you were involved in.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interviewed General Krstic. I was part of the interview, but that was after he was indicted. I don't recall interviewing the suspects who were ultimately charged before this Tribunal. I don't believe that someone I interviewed as a suspect became an indictee.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. According the -- or, rather, in the procedure prior to the point where an individual would be -- or could be given the status of a suspect, in that previous procedure, is any sort of pressure or influence exerted on the individual? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't really understand your question. Prior --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we were just now discussing cases of the procedure prior to the indictment being issued, that's to say, the procedure where you gathered information, would you tell individuals that they were suspects at that stage only in order to get information or answers that the Prosecution wanted to get? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If a person was a suspect, there was a valid reason that they were a suspect. It was complicated to conduct a taped interview. It was difficult to transcribe them. If I had an individual who was a witness, I would prefer that, because it was better for me to sit down with a witness and say, Tell me what happened, tell me the story. A suspect interview is more difficult to conduct, takes longer, and is by the nature of it, somewhat adversarial. If a witness was available, I would interview them as a witness, whether they be a Serb -- Bosnian Serb officer, or a civilian, or a Muslim, or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with any case where members of your team of investigators would be called to account for certain omissions on their part, for instance, for not investigating certain matters that were relevant or important? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so. You'd have to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you order that a team be set up from among members of the Bosnian government who would be charged with further exhumations? Was it you who did that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not me. The exhumations and the recovery of bodies by the Bosnians had been occurring for some years before we handed over responsibility, and that was a government body, established by that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that you set up a team from the Bosnian government which conducted further exhumations of mass graves, and you oversaw that work. So it wasn't the Bosnian government that that team up. So my question is: Could the Serbian government set up a team that would investigate crimes at Srebrenica? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't think that you are correct in this statement. I recall that the witness said the Bosnian government set up this commission which was monitored and supervised by the OTP investigators. This is my recollection of what he said, but perhaps you can explain it further, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. The Bosnian commission was already in place. Following the 2001 hand-over, we created a team of ICTY staff members who monitored the Bosnian commission. They -- they went to the sites with them, they did the work together, and that was the OTP staff who monitored the work of the commission. But in answer to the question about a Serbian investigation, I believe that was the case. The Republika Srpska conducted an inquiry in relation to Srebrenica and produced a report, as did the Dutch government, as did, I think, the Americans, as did, clearly, the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you about parliamentary reports or political reports. Yesterday, you said that Madam Del Ponte, Madam Prosecutor, decided that exhumations should be handed over to the Bosnian government. So was it an initiative that came from the Bosnian government or were they actually handed over the entire exercise?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday I don't recall the specifics. But we handed over responsibility to the relevant government in that country, the Bosnian authorities, and we monitored those exhumations, and then, after that, they were monitored by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, does the OTP of this Tribunal have the right to entrust exhumations to a government that was a party to the conflict and to a non-governmental organisation dealing with missing persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it did, and it does. And, indeed, the Tribunal has handed over prosecution matters to the Serbian government, to the governments of Montenegro, Croatia, and Bosnia. I believe that we had the right to do so and that it was approved by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you know full well what my question is: Did you hand over to the Serbian government investigations concerning grave-sites found in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to answer the question as best I could. I've said that we handed over to the Bosnian government. We did not hand over to the Serbian government those details. I know that we handed over to the Serbian state details of investigations and prosecutions and that that state has successfully prosecuted people for the Srebrenica offences. But we handed over to the Bosnian government, the Bosnian state government, the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I do understand you as a police officer. But, tell me, did you hand over investigations to the Bosnian commission or was it handed over to any and all who could do anything about it, the exhumations, grave-sites, so any Bosnian entities that could have anything to do with the grave-sites you located? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was handed over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons who conducted exhumations, monitored by, initially, the ICTY, and then by ICMP. And also probably by PHR and perhaps other government -- non-government organisations. But we handed it over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we must have the second break now. Have you any idea how much time your cross-examination will take? Is it possible to finish today or will you need more time tomorrow? It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will finish today, soon after the break, in fact. I have several questions left for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to be precise about what we were saying, both you and me, please tell me, was it the Federal Commission for Missing Persons that was the only one authorised to exhume mass graves around Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following our hand-over of responsibility for those graves, my answer would be yes. But once we had handed them over, then that would have been in the hands of the Bosnian commission. But, as I understand it, the Bosnian commission have been exhuming the bodies with the assistance of ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the federal commission have exclusive authority and monopoly over the mass graves, the bodies, and the artefacts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes. If someone attempted to exhume the graves who was not the Bosnian government, I would assume the Bosnian government would have attempted to stop that. We would certainly have attempted to intervene if someone not authorised attempted to disturb the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we saw that it was the only one that was authorised after responsibility was transferred to it, tell me, was the commission also authorised to transfer its authorisations to others, in relation to the exhumation of mass graves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How can you then check and verify the accuracy of the work of the Commission for Missing Persons, and does it submit any reports to you? Does it report to you on whom they employed, what they were doing, et cetera? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not. Initially we monitored the exhumations and then it was conducted by the Bosnian state commission and ICMP. They provided us data and information, as in that material that I produced in my report. But they did not report to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that all the information, the evidence, et cetera, was verified exclusively by the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons and the ICMP? And does this mean that neither the OTP nor other organs of the court have any jurisdiction over them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian commission and ICMP are primarily interested in recovering the bodies, and not recovering the evidence. If evidence was recovered, when we monitored, we would seize that evidence or have it provided to us. If evidence was found during exhumations and was provided to us by ICMP, we would use that information. But the Bosnian commission is recovering bodies, not recovering evidence. And the ICMP are monitoring that process and identifying those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Bosnian commission answer to this Court and to the OTP in any way whatsoever? Is it responsible to this Court in any way whatsoever? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. Apart from the Court's powers to subpoena witnesses or seek documents, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The authorisation of the Court or the OTP? Did the Court authorise the Bosnian commission or was it the OTP that authorised them?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the Court. It was the OTP and the ICTY that released responsibility for those mass graves to the Bosnian commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could then any information and any data entered by the Bosnian commission based on exhumation be considered impartial if you entrusted all of this to just one state or to just one party to the conflict, in relation to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have examined the work the Bosnian commission but, more particularly, the ICMP, and I believe the ICMP is an international body which is unconnected to the war and the conflict. I saw no evidence that there was any wrong-doing from the Bosnian commission in the recovery of the bodies, in the identification of the bodies, and in my review of ICMP procedures, or the Podrinje Identification Project procedures, I saw fairness, I saw checks and balances and review and a process which was predominantly geared to identifying the human remains and returning them to the families. They were very precise in their work. And, as I've indicated, I believe that they also recover bodies from the other entities, not just the Bosnian Muslim victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the working language of the commission? If it's the Bosnian state commission, what is its working language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the very end of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer the question, as I understood it, the working language of the commission would be B/C/S, Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian. And the main language utilized by ICMP was English. But they were multi-nationals, so I'm sure they used other languages. Documentation that I reviewed was either in B/C/S or was in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We would like to know how the OTP monitors the work of the Bosnian commission, if all its documents are in the Serbian language, or the Bosnian language, as they call it. How can they monitor it then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to ask the OTP if they continue to monitor the work of ICMP. I can simply state that if documents are received in a foreign language, they can be translated into English. Much of the reporting that I saw from ICMP was in English, and, indeed, many of the people employed there were former ICTY archaeologists or anthropologists or international anthropologists, archaeologists who produced documents in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you about the Bosnian commission, and then we'll get to the international commission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Bosnian commission and ICMP work together, so when they go to a site, they're together. They're in the same vehicles. They dig the same hole. They remove the same bodies. They work together. So, therefore, they, on occasion, produce documents in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the International Commission for Missing Persons have any responsibility to this Tribunal and to this Court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure of their mandate. They're an internationally recognised organisation. They may be signatory to some agreements. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether you saw a document today which had 220 names on it as victims of Srebrenica, and who were, in fact, killed before or after the events in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to the part of Mr. Helge Brunborg's report, in which there was -- stated 220 names, some of whom had been corrected, and some who had different dates. As I said, I'm not familiar with that document or the sources of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is anyone going to answer for the fact that they're trying to delude the Court by false entries and by entering people on these lists who were not killed in Srebrenica but after the events, in fact? At events later and at events that pre-date 1994? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you explain that? I'm -- I'm -- I don't understand your question. The fact that they are trying to delude the Court by false entries and by entering people on these lists who were not killed in Srebrenica but after the events. I'm surprised about this statement. You should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, let me rephrase my question. After the Brunborg report on irregularities in relation to a certain number of people, and based on their own findings, where the OTP found that false information was entered, does the OTP plan to start any proceedings against anyone in the Bosnian commission or in the ICMP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you know this witness is no longer part of the OTP or engaged with the -- or employed by the OTP. I think he can't answer the question about plans of the OTP. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I don't have any problem with the General putting his case as he is, that there has been false and there has been deluding and that kind of thing. But it needs to be done, of course, with something that serious to the -- to the person that he is suggesting that is doing it. And I'm not sure who he's suggesting, if it is Brunborg or someone else. But, yeah, no problem with his allegations which he has some sport for, which I don't think he does. But it should be done to the person or entity that he is accusing of such outrageous conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why I asked Mr. Tolimir to substantiate, clarify this allegation, how we should understand it. But it's in your hands to do that. Otherwise, please continue your cross-examination, if you have further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Manning, is this: Since you transferred authorities to the Bosnian government and to a non-governmental commission whereby they can decide what is a fair standard, did you maintain the right, as the OTP to hold anyone, either of them responsible for entering false information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness could answer the question for the time-period when he was employed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't believe there was specific content in the hand-over document that prescribed what they would do in that instance. It was outlined what we would ask them to do, as in provide us access to the sites, provide us information when necessary. I don't recall anything about sanctions if they provided false information. I would have to check the particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manning. During today's cross-examination, when I asked why you handed things over to Amor Masovic. He said it wasn't handed over to Mr. Amor Masovic but to Mr. Murat Hurtic. However, we have a document that we received by the OTP on the 7th of February, 2001, and I would like to have it shown to you a document in closed session so you could have a look at it and so that could you see that this document was sent to Amor Masovic with persons who signed their names on it, and I don't want to say these names until we're in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we go into closed session, I would just ask you -- I recall the witness having said that this responsibility was handed over to the Bosnian government, not to a single person. I think we should be clear with that. And now we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we give you the floor, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a clarification at page 78 of today's transcript, lines 2 to 6, you have -- you are recorded as having said the following: "To my recollection all the mass graves were located in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps within the Drina valley in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik, stretching from Pilica and the Branjevo Farm in the north, to Zeleni Jadar, secondary graves in the south. Is this -- are these places you are mentioning in Republika Srpska or in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I confused you, Your Honour. They are in, as I understood, the area of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, Mr. McCloskey. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't anticipate having a lot of redirect, but certainly more than about three minutes. If I can have some time to gather my thoughts, and there are some issues I want to discuss with Mr. Gajic which may make things go quicker. I have a question or two on this document so we can get that out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may do that. Otherwise it is better to commence the re-examination tomorrow. Because this courtroom is occupied this afternoon, and two of the three Judges present are sitting this afternoon in other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, have you to come back tomorrow; I apologise for that. We -- I have to remind you not to contact the parties during the break. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom, 2.15. We adjourn.
